_note: Global 10R scenario questions: Will's first working set (12 items) for founding-1789, 2026-09-21, reshaped from his proposed fields into the engine's: type vocab/move becomes choice/written by what the item asks for, resolution becomes the correct option or the exemplar, and his term/move/umbrella fields are kept as desk notes (underscored) because none of them is said to a student. Order is load-bearing - append only. His ' -- ' dashes are kept verbatim here and render as em dashes.

on_resolve._note: What resolving a question gives the town: a small drop in unrest, less for every hint used (the costed-hint model, as an in-fiction cost since the build has no equilibrium score), and one bounded bend - a town that understands how it is governed pays its taxes a little less grudgingly. Engineering defaults chosen by the build session 2026-09-21, not content and not a balance pass.

items.prompt: A philosophe argues that no king granted you the right to your own life and liberty -- you were born with it. Name the term for a right that exists before any government and isn't given by one.
hints: Think about where the right comes from -- a ruler, or something older than any ruler.
The term starts with the idea that some rights exist before government does.
It's the pair of words Locke used to argue government exists to protect, not to grant.

items.prompt: Explain, in one sentence, why people would voluntarily give up some of their freedom to a government at all.
hints: This isn't about fear of the ruler. It's about a trade the people choose to make.
The word you want pairs 'social' with a word for a binding agreement.
It's the deal Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau all describe differently but all name the same way.
items.exemplar: They trade some freedom for protection of their rights -- that trade is the social contract.
checklist: It says people give up something — some of their freedom.
It says what they get back — protection of their rights.
It treats it as a trade people agree to, not something forced on them.

items.prompt: A government changes its tax law. Under what condition does the Enlightenment argument say that law is legitimate?
hints: Legitimacy here isn't about force. It's about agreement.
Whose agreement has to be present for power to be legitimate?
Three words: consent... of the...?
items.exemplar: Only if the people being governed have agreed to be ruled by that government -- consent of the governed.
checklist: It says legitimacy comes from agreement, not force.
It names whose agreement counts — the people being governed.

items.prompt: Your Minister just told you: 'They're starting to ask whether obedience was ever the same as consent.' Name the pattern this line is pointing at -- not the event, the issue underneath it.
hints: Don't describe what's happening in the town. Name what's always at stake when a line like this gets said.
This is the same question every government has had to answer since the town's founding.
It's the umbrella issue this whole founding choice sits under: Power and Its ______.
items.exemplar: Power and its legitimacy -- whether a government's authority is real just because people obey it, or only when they've actually agreed to it.
checklist: It names an issue, not an event in the town.
It connects obeying to agreeing — whether the government's power is legitimate.

items.prompt: Unrest rose the week after you raised taxes. Is that proof the tax caused the unrest? Explain in one sentence what more you'd need to know.
hints: Something happening after something else isn't enough on its own.
What's the difference between something following an event and being caused by it?
The move here has a name: don't confuse timing with causation.
items.exemplar: No -- 'after' isn't 'because.' You'd need to rule out other causes happening the same week before you can call the tax the cause.
checklist: It says that one thing coming after another isn't proof it caused it.
It names what else you'd need to check or rule out.

items.prompt: Two advisors give you opposite readings of the same unrest. Before you decide who's right, what's the first thing you should ask about each of them?
hints: The content of what they say matters less right now than something else about them.
Ask about the speaker, not just the statement.
Say who said it -- and why that changes things.
items.exemplar: Who they are and why their position might shape what they're telling you -- who's speaking, and what they want.
checklist: It asks who each advisor is.
It asks why their position might shape what they tell you.

items.prompt: The Town Crier's announcement is written very differently from your Minister's private report. Why would the same information be phrased two different ways?
hints: Who is each one actually written for?
What does each speaker want the audience to do or feel?
Purpose and ______ -- the second word is who's listening.
items.exemplar: Because they're written for different audiences with different purposes -- a public announcement and a private advisory don't need to say the same thing the same way.
checklist: It names who each message is written for.
It says what each speaker wants their audience to do or feel.

items.prompt: Rousseau's rule isn't 'whatever the majority wants right now.' What is it instead?
hints: It's not the same as majority opinion -- that's a different term (will of all).
Think 'common good,' not 'most votes.'
Two words, and the first one means 'shared by everyone.'
items.exemplar: The general will -- what's genuinely in the shared interest of the whole community, not just the sum of individual wants.
checklist: It separates the general will from whatever most people want right now.
It says what the general will is — the shared interest of the whole community.

items.prompt: 'The old system had to go because it no longer served the people.' Is that reason enough, or does it go too far? Explain.
hints: A reason can be true and still be incomplete on its own.

checklist: It says whether the reason holds up on its own.
It says what evidence you'd need to back it up.

items.prompt: A ruler claims their authority comes directly from God and cannot be questioned by any court or assembly. Name both the claim and the system it justifies.
hints: One term is the justification, the other is the government it's used to defend.
Divine ______ justifies absolute ______.
This is Hobbes' pole, taken to its most extreme historical form.
items.exemplar: Divine right justifies absolute monarchy -- the claim, and the system it defends.
checklist: It names the claim the ruler makes.
It names the system of government that claim is used to defend.
